title: 802.11 MAC: how stations take turns
excerpt: CSMA/CA, backoff, collisions, hidden nodes and where the airtime of a frame really goes.
content:
A Wi-Fi radio cannot listen while it transmits, so it cannot detect collisions the way old wired Ethernet did. It tries to avoid them, and a large share of the time on every channel goes on that avoidance.

16 / 9 µsSIFS and slot time, OFDM at 20 MHz
10 / 20 µsSIFS and slot time, DSSS / CCK
15 to 1023contention window range (OFDM)
about 30 Mbit/sreal throughput of a 54 Mbit/s link

1. DefinitionWhat does the MAC do?

The medium access control (MAC) layer decides who may transmit, builds the frames and checks that they arrive. The basic rule of 802.11 is CSMA/CA (carrier sense multiple access with collision avoidance), implemented as the distributed coordination function (DCF).

  • Carrier sense. Listen before sending. The channel is busy if the radio hears a valid Wi-Fi signal or enough energy. A NAV (network allocation vector) timer also marks the channel busy for the duration written in a frame header.
  • Interframe spaces. A station waits a short time before it acts. SIFS (the shortest) is used before an acknowledgement; DIFS = SIFS + 2 slots is used before a new transmission.
  • Backoff. After DIFS the station waits a random number of idle slots, counting down while the channel is idle, then sends.
  • Acknowledgement. The receiver answers every unicast frame with an ACK after a SIFS. No ACK means the sender doubles its contention window and tries again.
  • Frame types. Management frames (beacons, authentication), control frames (RTS, CTS, ACK) and data frames.

2. PurposeWhy waiting is necessary

Wi-Fi is half duplex and the radio medium is shared by everyone within range. Two stations that talk at the same moment spoil both frames. Random backoff spreads the stations out in time so that, most of the time, only one of them sends in each slot.

3. MechanismContention and collisions

The simulation keeps every station saturated: each always has a frame to send. Add stations and watch what happens to the share of transmissions that collide and the time lost to them.

[wifi_lab model="csma" label="DCF contention and collisions"]

Try this. (1) With 2 stations, note the collision rate. Raise it to 10 and then 30. (2) Change aCWmin from 15 to 31 and see how a larger window trades fewer collisions for more idle time. (3) Use longer frames and notice that each collision then costs more.

4. VisualWhere the airtime goes

Even a station that has the channel to itself spends most of every frame on overheads. The bar shows one complete frame exchange: DIFS, average backoff, preamble, data, SIFS and acknowledgement. Only the green part is your data.

[wifi_lab model="airtime" label="Airtime of one frame exchange"]
PHY (20 MHz)SIFSSlotDIFS = SIFS + 2 x slotaCWmin
DSSS / HR-DSSS (802.11b)10 µs20 µs50 µs31
ERP (802.11g), long slot10 µs20 µs50 µs31 for DSSS / CCK, 15 for OFDM
ERP (802.11g), short slot10 µs9 µs28 µs15 for OFDM
OFDM (802.11a, 5 GHz)16 µs9 µs34 µs15

From IEEE Std 802.11-2020, Tables 16-4, 17-21 and 18-5 (characteristics of the HR/DSSS, OFDM and ERP PHYs). aCWmax is 1023 for all of them.

5. MathematicsThe overhead, with numbers

  • Contention window. The backoff is a random whole number of slots from 0 to CW, so on average CW / 2 slots. CW starts at aCWmin, becomes 2 × CW + 1 after each failure (15, 31, 63, 127 ... 1023) and returns to aCWmin after a success.
  • One frame exchange, OFDM 54 Mbit/s, 1500 bytes: DIFS 34 µs + average backoff 67.5 µs + preamble and signal field 20 µs + data 228 µs + SIFS 16 µs + ACK at 24 Mbit/s 28 µs = 393.5 µs, which delivers 12 000 bits, or 30.5 Mbit/s: 56% of the headline rate.
  • The same at 6 Mbit/s: 2225.5 µs for the frame exchange: 5.4 Mbit/s, which is 90% of the rate, because the data part is now long compared with the fixed overheads. Slow stations take a lot of airtime.
  • 802.11b, 11 Mbit/s, 1500 bytes: 1922 µs, 6.2 Mbit/s: 57% of the rate; at 1 Mbit/s it is 0.92 Mbit/s and takes 13 ms of airtime for one frame.
  • Small packets are worst: a 100-byte payload at 54 Mbit/s delivers just 4.3 Mbit/s, since the fixed overhead of about 185 µs dwarfs the data.

Quality of service: EDCA

802.11e added four access categories with different waiting rules. A higher-priority category waits less (a smaller AIFSN) and draws from a smaller contention window, so it wins more often:

Access categoryAIFSNCWminCWmax
Background (AC_BK)7151023
Best effort (AC_BE)3151023
Video (AC_VI)2715
Voice (AC_VO)237

Default values for OFDM PHYs (aCWmin 15, aCWmax 1023) from Table 9-155 of IEEE Std 802.11-2020. The access point can announce different values to its clients.

See the next topic, QoS and WMM: who goes first, for a step-by-step story, the priority labels and how to find them in a capture.

6. Real-world behaviourHidden nodes, slow clients and aggregation

Two clients on opposite sides of an access point may not hear each other, so carrier sensing cannot work between them. Their frames collide at the access point. Switching on RTS/CTS lets the access point's CTS reserve the channel for both.

[wifi_lab model="hidden" label="The hidden node problem"]
  • Slow clients cost everyone. A frame sent at 6 Mbit/s occupies the channel nine times as long as one at 54 Mbit/s, so a single poor client reduces the throughput of all the others. Disabling the lowest data rates on an access point keeps such clients from connecting at rates that waste airtime.
  • Aggregation. 802.11n introduced A-MPDU: many frames are sent behind one preamble and acknowledged together with a Block Ack, which recovers much of the overhead shown above.
  • Retries show waste. A frame that is sent again uses airtime twice. A retry rate above about 10 to 15% is a common warning level in practice, though no standard sets it.
  • Protection. In a 2.4 GHz network with 802.11b devices, newer devices send protection frames at slow rates first, costing yet more airtime.

Practical validationProve it in a capture and on a spectrum analyser

Reading about a band is one thing; seeing it in your own evidence is the skill. These checks work with any monitor-mode capture:

  • Filter on retried frames with wlan.fc.retry == 1 and compare their count with all data frames.
  • Find RTS, CTS and ACK frames: wlan.fc.type_subtype == 0x001b (RTS), 0x001c (CTS), 0x001d (ACK), 0x0019 (Block Ack). Check the duration field (wlan.duration) that sets the NAV.
  • Question to answer: a station sends at 6 Mbit/s and another at 54 Mbit/s, each the same frame size. How much more airtime does the slow one take per frame, ignoring overhead?

title: QoS and WMM: who goes first
excerpt: How four access categories give calls and video a head start over downloads, and where to see it in a capture.
content:
Your Wi-Fi carries calls, films, web pages and backups at the same time. Quality of service is how the network decides who goes first when they all want the air at once.

4waiting lines: voice, video, normal, background
0 to 7the priority label on every packet
47.5 to 146.5 µsaverage wait, voice to background
802.11ethe amendment that added it

In plain words. Think of four queues at a theme park. The fast-track queue waits a little less than the others, so VIPs usually get on the ride first, but only when the park is busy. Each packet wears a number that says which queue it joins.

[wifi_lab model="journeyqos" band="qos" label="Watch it happen: QoS and WMM"]

Where it livesWhich protocol, which layer, which frame

QuestionAnswer
Which standard added it?IEEE 802.11e (2005), now part of the base standard, IEEE Std 802.11-2020, where it is called EDCA (enhanced distributed channel access). The Wi-Fi Alliance certification name is WMM (Wi-Fi Multimedia).
Which layer?The MAC layer (channel access). The priority label starts higher up, in the IP header (DSCP) or a VLAN tag, and is copied into the MAC header by the sender.
Which frame carries it?Every QoS Data frame: a 2-byte QoS Control field in the MAC header holds the label. The access point’s waiting rules are announced in the Beacon, Probe Response and Association Response, in the EDCA Parameter Set element (element ID 12).
Which Wi-Fi generations?Wi-Fi 4 (802.11n) and later devices are QoS devices by definition, so Wi-Fi 4, 5, 6, 6E and 7. Older 802.11a/b/g devices only have it if they were WMM certified.
Anything new in Wi-Fi 6?MU EDCA (802.11ax): the access point can make a station wait longer after it has been served in a multi-user transmission, so one device cannot hog the air.

1. DefinitionWhat is QoS in Wi-Fi?

EDCA keeps the normal Wi-Fi rule (listen first, wait, then send, as in the MAC topic) but runs it four times in parallel, once per access category. Each category has its own waiting rules, so voice usually beats video, video beats normal traffic and normal traffic beats background.

2. PurposeWhy not treat everything the same?

Wi-Fi is shared, so every device waits for its turn. A call that waits too long breaks up, while a backup that waits a second is unnoticed. EDCA gives delay-sensitive traffic a head start without any central control.

3. MechanismThe label, the four lines and the waiting rules

The sender puts a user priority (0 to 7) on each packet. It decides the access category:

User priorityName used by WiresharkAccess categoryTypical traffic
1, 2Background, SpareBackground (AC_BK)backups, bulk transfers
0, 3Best Effort, Excellent EffortBest effort (AC_BE)web, email, anything unlabelled
4, 5Controlled Load, VideoVideo (AC_VI)streaming and conferencing video
6, 7Voice, Network ControlVoice (AC_VO)voice calls

Each category waits AIFS = SIFS + AIFSN × slot, then counts down a random backoff from 0 to CWmin. These are the defaults for OFDM PHYs; the access point can announce others.

Access categoryAIFSNCWminCWmaxAverage wait
Voice23747.5 µs
Video271565.5 µs
Best effort3151023110.5 µs
Background7151023146.5 µs

From IEEE Std 802.11-2020, Table 9-155, with SIFS 16 µs and slot 9 µs (OFDM, 20 MHz). Average wait = SIFS + AIFSN × slot + (CWmin / 2) × slot. The standard also gives each category a TXOP limit, the longest time it may keep the channel; it is not shown here.

Try this. In the player, change what you are doing, then press “Run another race” several times. The call line wins most races, but not every one: the priority is statistical, not a guarantee.

4. MathematicsWorking out the wait

  • Voice: 16 + 2 × 9 = 34 µs fixed, plus on average 3 / 2 = 1.5 slots = 13.5 µs, so 47.5 µs.
  • Background: 16 + 7 × 9 = 79 µs fixed, plus 15 / 2 = 7.5 slots = 67.5 µs, so 146.5 µs.
  • The difference is about 99 µs per turn. That is tiny, but when ten devices compete for hundreds of turns a second, the lines with the smaller waits win far more of them.

5. Real-world behaviourWhy a label does not always help

  • Nothing happens on a quiet network. With no competition everyone sends at once.
  • Many apps never set a label. Everything then lands in best effort and the voice and video lines stay empty.
  • Routers can rewrite the label. The common shortcut of using the top three bits of the DSCP value as the Wi-Fi priority sends EF (DSCP 46, the usual voice marking) to priority 5, video. RFC 8325 recommends a mapping that sends it to 6.
  • It only applies on the Wi-Fi hop. The label does nothing for congestion elsewhere on the path, such as your internet connection.
  • Turn WMM on. On most access points it is on by default; turning it off can also limit the link speed of newer devices.

In your captureWhere to find it and how to filter it

These filters were tested with TShark 4.6 on a hand-built capture file with the same frame layout. Check them on your own capture and version, and remember that a monitor-mode capture only shows what your adapter heard.

What you want to seeWhich frame and elementDisplay filter
Packets that use QoS at allQoS Data frames (type/subtype 0x28). Plain Data frames are 0x20.wlan.fc.type_subtype == 0x0028
The priority of each packetQoS Data frame → QoS Control → Priority and TID. Right-click Priority and choose Apply as Column.wlan.qos.priority == 6
wlan.qos.priority >= 4
How the packet is acknowledgedQoS Control → Ack Policy (0 normal, 1 none, 3 Block Ack).wlan.qos.ack == 3
The access point’s waiting rulesBeacon or Association Response → EDCA Parameter Set → one Ac Parameters entry per category: AIFSN, ECWmin/ECWmax, TXOP limit.wlan.fc.type_subtype == 0x0008 && wlan.tag.number == 12
The same rules as WMMThe vendor-specific WMM/WME Parameter Element (Wi-Fi Alliance) in the same frames.wlan.wfa.ie.wme.subtype
The MU EDCA rules (Wi-Fi 6)Beacon → MU EDCA Parameter Set extension element.wlan.ext_tag.mu_edca_parameter_set.mu_edca_timer
The IP-level labelThe IP header, only visible on a wired capture or after decryption. Over the air, WPA2 and WPA3 hide it.ip.dsfield.dscp == 46
  • Healthy: voice and video apps show priority 5 or 6, ordinary browsing shows 0, and the beacon lists four categories with voice and video using the smaller values.
  • Problem: everything shows priority 0 (the label is missing or was rewritten), or the beacon has no EDCA element (the network is not using WMM).
  • Reading the beacon: Wireshark shows the contention window as an exponent (ECW). CWmin = 2ECWmin − 1, so ECWmin 4 means 15. The TXOP limit is in units of 32 µs, and 0 means one frame.
  • Question: a call app is marked DSCP 46 on the laptop, but the Wi-Fi capture shows priority 5. Where did the label change?

title: Frames and the MAC header: what each protocol adds
excerpt: The MAC header of every 802.11 protocol, field by field, with sizes, bits, PHY preambles and aggregation.
content:
Every Wi-Fi generation changed what a frame looks like. This topic lets you build the MAC header of each protocol, field by field, and see what was added, how many bytes it costs and why.

24 bytesMAC header of a plain data frame
+2 / +4 bytesQoS Control (802.11e) and HT Control (802.11n)
14 bytesthe shortest frames: ACK and CTS
4 bytesFCS at the end of every frame

1. DefinitionFrames, MSDUs and PPDUs

  • MSDU (MAC service data unit): the payload handed down from the layer above, for example an IP packet with its 8-byte LLC/SNAP header. Up to 2304 bytes.
  • MPDU (MAC protocol data unit): the real MAC frame: MAC header, frame body and FCS. This is what Wireshark calls an 802.11 frame.
  • A-MSDU / A-MPDU: several MSDUs inside one frame, or several MPDUs sent back to back (aggregation, from 802.11n).
  • PSDU (PHY service data unit): what the PHY carries, which is one MPDU or an A-MPDU.
  • PPDU (PHY protocol data unit): the PSDU with the PHY preamble in front of it. This is what actually goes on the air.
  • FCS (frame check sequence): a 32-bit CRC at the end of the MPDU.

The three kinds of frame

  • Management frames set up and manage the network: beacons, probes, authentication, association, deauthentication.
  • Control frames help deliver the others: RTS, CTS, ACK, Block Ack, and in 802.11ax the Trigger frame. They are short and have no sequence number.
  • Data frames carry user traffic (and QoS Data frames carry a priority).

2. PurposeWhy the header looks like this

The header answers four questions for the receiver, in as few bytes as possible: who is this for and from (addresses), what kind of frame is it (Frame Control), how long will the channel be busy (Duration), and is this a repeat (Sequence Control). Each new generation added only the fields it needed (priority, then feedback for beamforming), and kept the rest the same so that old and new devices could share a channel.

3. MechanismBuild the header of each protocol

Choose a protocol and a frame type. The boxes are the real fields in transmission order, with their widths in bytes. Orange-edged boxes are fields that this protocol added. Click any box for its meaning and its bits; switch To DS and From DS on a data frame to see the addresses change meaning.

[wifi_lab model="macframe" label="MAC header builder for each protocol"]

Try this. (1) Choose QoS Data and move from 802.11e to 802.11n and tick +HTC: the header grows from 26 to 30 bytes. (2) Choose Data and turn both To DS and From DS on: a fourth address appears. (3) Click Beacon and step from 802.11 to 802.11ac: the frame body gains the HT and VHT elements. (4) Choose Trigger in 802.11ax and add clients: each one costs 5 bytes. (5) Click Frame Control and step through the protocols: the last bits and the list of frame subtypes change with each one.

4. VisualWhat changed from protocol to protocol

ProtocolWhat it added to framesCost
802.11 (1997), b, a, gFrame Control, Duration, three addresses, Sequence Control, FCS; an optional fourth address for bridges and mesh; RTS, CTS, ACK24-byte header (30 with a fourth address)
802.11e (QoS)QoS Control field in QoS Data frames: traffic identifier, ack policy, A-MSDU present, queue size; Block Ack. Frame Control: subtype bit 7 becomes the QoS flag (new QoS data subtypes); new Block Ack Request and Block Ack subtypes+2 bytes
802.11n (Wi-Fi 4)HT Control field (+HTC); A-MSDU and A-MPDU aggregation; compressed Block Ack; HT elements in management frames. Frame Control: the Order bit becomes +HTC; new Control Wrapper and Action No Ack subtypes+4 bytes; +28 and +24 bytes of elements in a beacon
802.11ac (Wi-Fi 5)VHT variant of the HT Control field; larger MPDUs (up to 11 454 bytes) and A-MPDUs (up to 1 048 575 bytes); VHT elements. Frame Control: new Beamforming Report Poll and VHT NDP Announcement subtypessame 4 bytes; +14 and +7 bytes of elements
802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6)HE variant of the HT Control field (a list of small control items); Trigger frame; HE elements. Frame Control: a new Trigger subtypesame 4 bytes; Trigger frame 28 + 5 per client
802.11be (Wi-Fi 7)Extends the same header and control items; EHT elements; larger aggregatessame 4 bytes

The HE and EHT details come from the 802.11ax and 802.11be amendments; the earlier rows are from IEEE Std 802.11-2020.

The Frame Control field changes too. It is always 16 bits, but each protocol claimed unused subtype values for its new frames, the Order bit became +HTC in 802.11n, and the WEP bit was renamed Protected Frame. Click Frame Control in the builder above and switch protocol to see the bits and the list of subtypes change. The 2020 edition of the standard no longer lists the point-coordination (PCF) data subtypes such as Data + CF-Poll: they were defined in 1997 but are now reserved, so the builder dims them.

Who is Address 1, 2, 3 and 4?

The same three address fields change meaning with the To DS and From DS bits, depending on whether the frame is going into or out of the access point. This is the table from the standard (Table 9-30):

To DSFrom DSAddress 1Address 2Address 3Address 4
00Destination (receiver)Source (transmitter)BSSIDnot present
01Destination (receiver)BSSID (the AP, transmitter)Sourcenot present
10BSSID (the AP, receiver)Source (transmitter)Destinationnot present
11ReceiverTransmitterDestinationSource

A client sending to the access point uses 1 / 0. The access point forwarding to a client uses 0 / 1. 1 / 1 is used between access points in a bridge or mesh, which is the only reason a fourth address exists.

5. MathematicsSizes and overhead

  • Header length = 24 + 6 (if To DS and From DS are both 1) + 2 (if QoS Data) + 4 (if +HTC). Management frames are 24 bytes (+4 with +HTC).
  • Control frames: RTS 20 bytes (Frame Control 2, Duration 2, two addresses 12, FCS 4); CTS and ACK 14 bytes; Block Ack 32 bytes in its compressed form (152 bytes in the original 802.11e form with a 128-byte bitmap); a Trigger frame 28 + 5 × (number of clients) bytes.
  • Security overhead: TKIP adds 20 bytes (8-byte IV, 8-byte MIC, 4-byte ICV), CCMP-128 adds 16 (8-byte header and 8-byte MIC), CCMP-256 24, GCMP 24 (8-byte header and a 16-byte MIC), WEP 8.
  • Overhead of one frame = (header + security + FCS) / frame size. For a QoS Data frame with CCMP, the overhead is 26 + 16 + 4 = 46 bytes: 3.0% of a frame carrying 1500 bytes, but 31% of one carrying 100 bytes.
  • An A-MSDU subframe is a 14-byte header (destination 6, source 6, length 2), the MSDU, and padding to a multiple of 4 bytes. An A-MPDU subframe is a 4-byte delimiter (1 + 1 + 14 + 8 + 8 bits: end-of-frame flag, reserved, MPDU length, CRC, and the signature 0x4E), the MPDU, and padding to a multiple of 4.
LimitSize
MSDU and management frame body2304 bytes
A-MSDU (802.11n)3839 or 7935 bytes
MPDU (802.11ac)3895, 7991 or 11 454 bytes
PSDU (802.11n)65 535 bytes
PSDU (802.11ac)4 692 480 bytes

From IEEE Std 802.11-2020, Table 9-25. A larger frame is a bigger gamble: one bit error in it spoils the whole frame, unless the frames are aggregated as separate MPDUs.

6. Real-world behaviourThe preamble and aggregation

The MAC header is only half the story. In front of every frame the PHY adds a preamble. The first part is always the legacy preamble, so that any device can read the length and stay quiet; later generations add their own fields behind it, and the preamble grows with the number of spatial streams.

[wifi_lab model="ppdu" label="PHY preambles of each protocol"]

Each frame also pays for waiting for the channel and for its acknowledgement, which is why aggregation was invented. An A-MSDU shares one header across several packets; an A-MPDU keeps a header for each frame but shares the preamble, the wait and the acknowledgement.

[wifi_lab model="aggregation" label="Aggregation: A-MSDU and A-MPDU"]

Worked example. Eight packets of 300 bytes at 300 Mbit/s, QoS Data with CCMP. Sent as eight separate frames, they take about 1528 µs and deliver 4% of the data rate. As an A-MSDU they take about 252 µs (25%), and as an A-MPDU about 262 µs (24%): six times faster, from the same radio, just by not repeating the wait, the preamble and the acknowledgement.

  • Retries show up in the header. The Retry bit and the repeated sequence number tell you which frames were sent again.
  • Mixed networks pay too. To keep old devices quiet, a newer frame starts with the legacy preamble and sometimes a protection exchange.
  • Capture tools add their own header. A monitor-mode capture starts every frame with a radiotap header (signal, rate, channel); that is not part of the 802.11 frame.

Practical validationProve it in a capture and on a spectrum analyser

Reading about a band is one thing; seeing it in your own evidence is the skill. These checks work with any monitor-mode capture:

  • In a capture, filter on each frame type with wlan.fc.type_subtype, for example 0x0008 for a beacon and 0x0028 for a QoS Data frame, and compare the header lengths. Open the Frame Control field and find the To DS and From DS bits (wlan.fc.ds).
  • Find a retry (wlan.fc.retry == 1) and look at its sequence number (wlan.seq): it repeats the number of the original.
  • Open a beacon and expand the tagged parameters: look for HT Capabilities (tag 45), VHT Capabilities (tag 191) and the HE and EHT capability elements, and add up their sizes.
  • Question to answer: a client's data frame to the access point has To DS = 1, From DS = 0. What would Address 3 hold if the client is browsing a website?

Check your understandingQuick quiz

  • IEEE Std 802.11-2020 (IEEE Xplore)
  • IEEE 802.11 Working Group: standards timelines (approval and publication dates)
  • Wireshark display filter reference: IEEE 802.11 (wlan)
  • Wireshark display filter reference: radiotap

Frame formats, field sizes and bit layouts were checked against IEEE Std 802.11-2020: Frame Control (Figures 9-3 and 9-4, subtype values in Table 9-1, +HTC and Protected Frame in 9.2.4.1.9 and 9.2.4.1.10), Sequence Control (9-7), QoS Control (Table 9-10), HT Control (Figures 9-11, 9-12 and 9-16), the address table (Table 9-30), size limits (Table 9-25), the A-MPDU delimiter (Table 9-527), A-MSDU subframes (Figure 9-69), CCMP and GCMP expansion (12.5.3 and 12.5.5) and the HT preamble timings (Table 19-6). HE and EHT items come from the 802.11ax and 802.11be amendments, which are not in the 2020 edition. Check Wireshark field names against your version.

title: Wi-Fi generations: from 802.11b to Wi-Fi 7
excerpt: What each generation added and how its headline speed is built, with an interactive explorer.
content:
Wi-Fi has changed shape many times since 1997. Each generation kept what worked and added one or two ideas. This topic maps those ideas and the headline speeds they allow.

11 Mbit/s802.11b, 1999
54 Mbit/s802.11a and g
6.9 Gbit/s802.11ac, theoretical
46 Gbit/s802.11be, theoretical

1. DefinitionStandards, amendments and names

  • IEEE 802.11 is the family of standards. Each new feature is an amendment (802.11b, g, n, ac, ax, be) which is later merged into a new revision of the base standard.
  • Wi-Fi Alliance names: Wi-Fi 4 (802.11n), Wi-Fi 5 (802.11ac), Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax), Wi-Fi 6E (Wi-Fi 6 in 6 GHz) and Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be). Older generations never had an official brand.
  • Certification by the Wi-Fi Alliance tests that devices interoperate. A standard being approved and a product being certified are separate events with different dates.

2. PurposeWhy there is a new generation

Every generation answers a limit of the one before: 802.11b needed more speed, 802.11g brought OFDM to 2.4 GHz, 802.11n added antennas, 802.11ac widened channels, 802.11ax fixed crowded networks, and 802.11be adds multi-link operation and very wide channels. A newer access point improves the experience of older clients less than people expect, because each client uses the best generation it supports.

3. MechanismExplore the generations

Click a generation to see its properties and how its top speed is built. Use the feature buttons to dim the generations that lack a feature.

[wifi_lab model="generations" label="Wi-Fi generations"]

4. VisualWhat each generation added

GenerationApprovedNew in this generation
802.11b1999CCK, 5.5 and 11 Mbit/s in 2.4 GHz
802.11a1999OFDM in 5 GHz, 54 Mbit/s
802.11g2003OFDM in 2.4 GHz, compatible with 802.11b
802.11n (Wi-Fi 4)2009MIMO (4 streams), 40 MHz channels, frame aggregation
802.11ac (Wi-Fi 5)201380 and 160 MHz channels, 256-QAM, downlink MU-MIMO, 5 GHz only
802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6, 6E)2021OFDMA, 1024-QAM, uplink MU-MIMO, BSS colouring, target wake time, 6 GHz
802.11be (Wi-Fi 7)2024320 MHz channels, 4096-QAM, multi-link operation, multi-RU and puncturing, 16 streams

Approval dates are from the IEEE 802.11 Working Group timelines; 802.11ac was approved in December 2013. 802.11bn (the working name for a following amendment, aimed at reliability) is in development.

5. MathematicsHow a headline speed is built

Highest rate = data subcarriers × bits per subcarrier × coding rate × spatial streams / symbol time, with the widest channel, the highest modulation and the most streams. For example:

  • 802.11a/g: 48 × 6 × 3/4 / 4 µs = 54 Mbit/s.
  • 802.11n: 108 × 6 × 5/6 × 4 / 3.6 µs = 600 Mbit/s (40 MHz, 4 streams, short guard interval).
  • 802.11ac: 468 × 8 × 5/6 × 8 / 3.6 µs = 6933 Mbit/s (160 MHz, 8 streams).
  • 802.11ax: 1960 × 10 × 5/6 × 8 / 13.6 µs = 9608 Mbit/s (160 MHz, 8 streams).
  • 802.11be: 3920 × 12 × 5/6 × 16 / 13.6 µs = 46 118 Mbit/s (320 MHz, 16 streams).

Read the number with care. These are theoretical physical-layer rates. A real phone with two antennas on an 80 MHz channel reaches a small fraction, and the airtime model in the MAC topic shows that about half of any link rate goes on overhead.

6. Real-world behaviourWhat users actually see

  • The client limits the link. Most phones have two antennas and a modest channel width, so the generation of the access point matters less than the client's.
  • Backward compatibility has a cost. Legacy rates and protection mechanisms use airtime. Turning off old rates in a network with only modern clients helps everyone.
  • Bands matter as much as generations. 6 GHz is only for 802.11ax and newer, which is why Wi-Fi 6E networks have no legacy clients.
  • Features need both ends. OFDMA, MU-MIMO, MLO and 4096-QAM only work when the client supports them too.

Practical validationProve it in a capture and on a spectrum analyser

Reading about a band is one thing; seeing it in your own evidence is the skill. These checks work with any monitor-mode capture:

  • In a beacon or an association request, find the HT Capabilities, VHT Capabilities and HE Capabilities elements to see which generations a device supports.
  • Compare the rates a 2x2 phone reaches on the same access point in 20, 40 and 80 MHz channels.
  • Question to answer: why is the highest 802.11ac rate in this topic not reachable on 2.4 GHz?

title: Spatial reuse and BSS colouring: sharing with your neighbours
excerpt: How Wi-Fi 6 tells a neighbour from your own network and lets routers talk at the same time, and where to see it in a capture.
content:
In a block of flats, dozens of Wi-Fi networks share the same few channels, and the old rule says to wait whenever you hear any of them. Wi-Fi 6 lets a router tell a neighbour from its own network, and sometimes talk at the same time.

1 to 63BSS colours (a 6-bit number)
−82 dBmdefault level below which a neighbour is ignored
up to −62 dBmhighest level a device may raise it to
802.11axWi-Fi 6, still used in Wi-Fi 7

In plain words. Imagine two classes sharing a hall, each wearing a different coloured bib. The old rule was: if anyone is talking, everyone stays silent. The new rule is: if the talker is wearing the other class’s colour and is far away, you may talk too, just a little more quietly.

[wifi_lab model="journeybss" band="bss" label="Watch it happen: BSS colouring"]

Where it livesWhich protocol, which layer, which frame

QuestionAnswer
Which standard added it?IEEE 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6), published as IEEE Std 802.11ax-2021. It is an amendment, so it is not in the 2020 base edition of the standard. Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be) keeps it.
Which layer?It starts in the PHY (the colour is in the HE-SIG-A field of the PHY header, read in the first moments of a packet) and it changes a MAC decision: whether to treat the channel as busy.
Which frame carries it?Every HE packet carries the colour in its PHY header, so it is not in the MAC header. The access point’s own colour is announced in the Beacon, Probe Response and Association Response, in the HE Operation element (BSS Color Information field).
Which Wi-Fi generations?Wi-Fi 6, 6E and 7 only. Older devices cannot read the colour and keep following the old rule.
Which bands?All bands that Wi-Fi 6 runs on: 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, and 6 GHz (Wi-Fi 6E).

1. DefinitionWhat are BSS colouring and spatial reuse?

A BSS (basic service set) is one access point and its clients. BSS colouring gives each BSS a number from 1 to 63 that every packet carries. Spatial reuse is what a device can do with it: it can ignore a packet from another BSS (an OBSS, an overlapping BSS) when that packet is weak enough, and transmit at the same time.

2. PurposeWhy waiting for the neighbour is a waste

Before Wi-Fi 6, every Wi-Fi signal above about −82 dBm made the channel look busy, whichever network sent it. In dense buildings that means routers wait for each other when their clients are far apart and would not disturb each other at all.

3. MechanismRead the colour, then decide

The packet heard is…Its level at my deviceWhat a Wi-Fi 6 device does
Same colour (my own network)anyTreat it as mine: wait my turn as usual.
Different colourbelow −82 dBmIgnore it, as the old rule already did.
Different colourbetween −82 dBm and my thresholdMay treat the channel as idle and transmit, with lower transmit power.
Different colourabove my thresholdWait: it is too loud to talk over.
Not Wi-Fi 6 (no colour)above −82 dBmWait, as before.

A device may raise its threshold from −82 dBm up to −62 dBm. The rule that keeps this fair: it must lower its transmit power by the same number of dB that it raised the threshold. The access point can also announce spatial reuse settings for its network in the Spatial Reuse Parameter Set element, including a group of friendly networks (an SRG) that may be more aggressive with each other.

Try this. In the player, scene 4: set the neighbour’s colour to different, then drag the loudness from faint to loud and watch the decision change. Then set the colour to the same as yours.

4. MathematicsThe power trade-off, with numbers

  • Raise the threshold from −82 to −72 dBm: that is 10 dB, so the device must lower its transmit power by 10 dB. A router sending at 20 dBm (100 mW) then sends at 10 dBm (10 mW).
  • Why it is fair: a transmitter that is 10 dB quieter disturbs the neighbour 10 times less, which is what you gave up by not waiting.
  • The cost: at 10 dB less power the client sees a weaker signal, so it may need a slower data rate. Spatial reuse pays off when the client is close to its own router and far from the neighbour.

5. Real-world behaviourWhat to expect

  • Gains depend on the building. Several networks, close together, with clients near their own routers, benefit most. A lone router benefits not at all.
  • Old devices drag it down. A neighbour’s Wi-Fi 5 device sends no colour, so Wi-Fi 6 devices still wait for it.
  • Colour collisions happen. Two neighbouring routers can choose the same colour. They then treat each other as one network. An access point can send a BSS Color Change Announcement and move to another colour.
  • Routers choose the colour themselves. Most home routers give you no setting for it.

In your captureWhere to find it and how to filter it

These filters were tested with TShark 4.6 on hand-built captures with the same element layout. Check them on your own capture and version. A colour per packet needs an adapter that records it, and many do not.

What you want to seeWhich frame and elementDisplay filter
The colour an access point usesBeacon or Association Response → HE Operation element → BSS Color Information → BSS Color.wlan.ext_tag.bss_color_information.bss_color == 12
Colour switched offThe same field group: BSS Color Disabled bit set while the colour is changing.wlan.ext_tag.bss_color_information.bss_color_disabled == 1
A colour change being announcedBeacon → BSS Color Change Announcement element: the new colour and a countdown of beacons.wlan.ext_tag.bss_color_change.new_bss_color
wlan.ext_tag.bss_color_change.color_switch_countdown
The network’s spatial reuse settingsBeacon → Spatial Reuse Parameter Set element (SR Control, OBSS PD offsets, SRG colour bitmap).wlan.ext_tag.spatial_reuse.sr_control
The colour of each packetNot in the MAC header. It is in the HE-SIG-A of the PHY header and appears in the radiotap HE field, only if the capture adapter reports it.radiotap.he.data_3.bss_color == 7
radiotap.he.data_1.bss_color_known == 1
  • Healthy: your access point uses one colour that differs from the neighbours’, and it does not keep changing.
  • Problem: two access points on the same channel announce the same colour (a collision), or the colour keeps changing between beacons.
  • Question: your capture shows no colour per packet at all. Is the network not using Wi-Fi 6, or is the capture adapter not recording it? Which frames help you decide?

The threshold used in the simulation (−72 dBm) is an illustration. Filter names were tested on hand-built captures.

title: Connecting and coexisting
excerpt: Joining a network, roaming, security and sharing spectrum.
content:
A Wi-Fi device has to find a network, prove it belongs, keep its connection as it moves, and live alongside everything else on the air. This part covers all four.

TopicsStart with the connection, then the neighbours

Joining and movingAssociationDiscovery, authentication, the four-way handshake, WPA3, roaming and sticky clients.Sharing spectrumCoexistenceInterference, Bluetooth and ZigBee, clear channel assessment and the rules in the UK, EU and US.

title: Association, security and roaming
excerpt: The connection sequence from beacon to encrypted data, WPA2 and WPA3, and why clients stick to distant access points.
content:
Before a single byte of your data moves, a device and an access point exchange a short, fixed conversation. Knowing its order is the fastest way to find out why a client will not connect.

4frame exchanges to join a WPA2 network: discover, authenticate, associate, handshake
102.4 msdefault beacon interval (100 time units)
15reason code for a failed four-way handshake
802.11k, v, rthe roaming helpers

Where it livesWhich protocol, which layer, which frame

QuestionAnswer
Which standards?Authentication and association are in the base IEEE 802.11 standard. WPA2 is the Wi-Fi Alliance name for the RSN security of IEEE 802.11i (2004). WPA3 (Wi-Fi Alliance, 2018) uses SAE, the “dragonfly” handshake, which is also part of the base standard. Roaming helpers 802.11k (neighbour reports), 802.11v (BSS transition requests) and 802.11r (fast transition) started as amendments and are now in the base standard.
Which layer?The MAC layer: management frames for joining and roaming. The four-way handshake that creates the encryption keys travels as EAPOL messages inside ordinary data frames.
Which frames carry it?Beacons and probe responses advertise the security (RSN element) and roaming support (mobility domain element). Then come Authentication, Association Request and Response, four EAPOL-Key messages, and for roaming Reassociation and Action frames.
Which Wi-Fi generations?All of them can join and use WPA2. WPA3 is required for Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 devices on 6 GHz, and available on newer Wi-Fi 6 devices. 802.11k, v and r are optional on any generation.

1. DefinitionThe words

  • Discovery: finding networks, by listening for beacons (passive scanning) or by sending probe requests (active scanning).
  • Authentication: in 802.11 terms a formal first step. Open-system authentication proves nothing; WPA3 uses it to carry the SAE exchange.
  • Association: the client joins the access point, which records its capabilities and gives it an association ID.
  • Key management: turning a password or an enterprise credential into the keys that encrypt the traffic.
  • Roaming: moving from one access point to another without losing the session. Steering is the access point or controller persuading a client to move.

2. PurposeWhat it protects against

Radio signals reach everyone nearby, so the network has to prove that a device is allowed in and keep what it sends private. Without encryption anyone in range can read the traffic and join the network. The handshake gives each client its own key, so one client cannot read another's traffic.

3. MechanismStep through the connection

Choose the type of network and click through each step. The diagram shows the frames, the card shows what they do, the Wireshark filter to find them and what failure looks like at that point.

[wifi_lab model="assoc" label="Connection sequence"]
SecurityIntroducedProtects withNotes
WPA2003TKIPA stop-gap for older hardware; no longer acceptable
WPA2 (IEEE 802.11i)2004AES-CCMP; four-way handshakePersonal (shared password) or Enterprise (802.1X / EAP)
WPA32018SAE for Personal; stronger keys for Enterprise; protected management framesRequired for Wi-Fi 6E and 6 GHz operation, together with Enhanced Open (OWE) for open networks

4. VisualRoaming and the sticky client

A client walks between two access points. It decides for itself when to roam. Raise the roaming threshold and the client moves earlier; lower it and the client holds on to the first access point long after the second is stronger.

[wifi_lab model="roaming" label="Roaming between two access points"]

5. MathematicsKeys and thresholds

  • Pairwise transient key. Both sides compute PTK = PRF(PMK, ANonce, SNonce, AP address, client address). The master key (PMK) comes from the password (Personal) or from 802.1X (Enterprise). The nonces are random numbers, so each connection gets fresh keys, and the key itself never crosses the air.
  • Roaming rule. A typical client roams when its signal drops below a threshold and a candidate is stronger by a margin: here, with the access points 40 m apart and a threshold of -70 dBm, the client holds on to the first access point for about 7 m beyond the halfway point. The model uses free-space loss at 5 GHz with an exponent of 3.
  • Beacon interval. The default is 100 time units; one time unit is 1024 µs, so 102.4 ms. A client scanning 13 channels spends at least that long on each channel to hear every beacon, which is why active scans and 802.11k neighbour lists matter.

6. Real-world behaviourFailures and fixes

Reason codeMeaningUsual cause
1Unspecified reasonAnything; look at what happened just before
2Previous authentication no longer validClient or AP lost its state, often after a restart or a roam
3Deauthenticated because the sender is leavingA client disconnecting normally
4Disassociated due to inactivityThe AP's idle timer expired, often a sleeping device
5AP unable to handle all current stationsThe AP is full
154-way handshake timeoutWrong password, or weak signal during the handshake
16Group key handshake timeoutClient stopped answering during a key update

Reason codes from IEEE Std 802.11-2020, Table 9-49.

  • Sticky clients. Raise the minimum rate or signal an access point will accept, enable 802.11k and 802.11v where the clients support them, and avoid power levels so high that a distant access point still looks strong.
  • Slow reconnects. A full re-authentication with 802.1X takes much longer than a handover with 802.11r (fast BSS transition), which carries the keys ahead.
  • Protected management frames (802.11w) stop spoofed deauthentication frames from forcing a client off; WPA3 and the 6 GHz band require them.

Practical validationProve it in a capture and on a spectrum analyser

Reading about a band is one thing; seeing it in your own evidence is the skill. These checks work with any monitor-mode capture:

  • Capture a client joining a network and find each step: wlan.fc.type_subtype == 0x000b (authentication), 0x0000 and 0x0001 (association request and response), eapol (the four-way handshake).
  • Walk between two access points with a laptop capturing and find the reassociation request (wlan.fc.type_subtype == 0x0002). Note the signal of the old access point at that moment.
  • Look for deauthentication (0x000c) and disassociation (0x000a) frames and read the reason code.
  • Question to answer: a client repeatedly fails with reason 15 on one SSID only. What is the first thing to check?

In your captureWhere to find each step and how to filter it

These filters were tested with TShark 4.6 on hand-built captures with the same frame layout. Check them on your own capture and version.

What you want to seeWhich frame and elementDisplay filter
The security a network offersBeacon or Probe Response → RSN element → Auth Key Management (AKM) Suite. Type 2 is WPA2-Personal (PSK), 8 is WPA3-Personal (SAE), 1 is 802.1X, 4 and 9 are fast-transition versions.wlan.rsn.akms.type == 8
A WPA3 (SAE) handshake startingAuthentication frame with algorithm 3 (SAE). Sequence 1 is the commit, 2 the confirm.wlan.fixed.auth.alg == 3
Joining and leavingAuthentication, Association Request and Response; a refusal shows a status code, a disconnect shows a reason code.wlan.fc.type_subtype == 0x000b
wlan.fixed.status_code != 0
wlan.fixed.reason_code
The four-way handshakeFour EAPOL-Key frames inside data frames. Wireshark numbers them 1 to 4.eapol
wlan_rsna_eapol.keydes.msgnr == 1
Fast roaming (802.11r) offeredBeacon → Mobility Domain element. Access points that share a mobility domain ID can do fast transitions.wlan.mobility_domain.mdid
An access point asking a client to move (802.11v)Action frame, category 10 (WNM), action 7: BSS Transition Management Request. Action 8 is the client’s answer.wlan.fixed.category_code == 10 && wlan.fixed.action_code == 7
A neighbour list (802.11k)Action frame, category 5 (Radio Measurement): action 4 asks for the list, action 5 answers.wlan.fixed.category_code == 5 && wlan.fixed.action_code == 5
The client actually movingReassociation Request (subtype 2). Compare the time between the last frame to the old access point and this frame.wlan.fc.type_subtype == 0x0002
  • Healthy: authentication, association and all four EAPOL messages appear within a fraction of a second, in order.
  • Problem: the handshake repeats (message 1 appears again and again: wrong password or a key mismatch), a status code is not 0, or a reason code appears right after the handshake.
  • Question: a phone sits on a weak access point and never moves. Which frames would show whether the network ever suggested a better one?

title: Coexistence and regulations
excerpt: Interference, clear channel assessment, Bluetooth and ZigBee, and the UK, EU and US rules for each band.
content:
Wi-Fi shares its spectrum with other Wi-Fi networks and with devices that do not speak Wi-Fi at all. How it behaves depends on whether it can understand the signal, and the law decides how loud it may be.

-82 dBmlevel at which Wi-Fi defers to a Wi-Fi signal (20 MHz)
-62 dBmlevel at which it defers to any energy
79Bluetooth channels, each 1 MHz wide
2 MHzwidth of a ZigBee channel

1. DefinitionKinds of interference

  • Co-channel interference: another Wi-Fi network on the same channel. Because Wi-Fi can decode it, the two share the airtime fairly: they take turns.
  • Adjacent-channel interference: a network on a nearby but not identical channel. The radio cannot decode its preamble, so it counts as noise, and the transmissions cannot take turns. This is worse than co-channel.
  • Non-Wi-Fi interference: Bluetooth, ZigBee, cordless phones, microwave ovens, baby monitors and poorly shielded electronics. They never take turns.
  • Hidden nodes: stations that cannot hear each other (see the MAC topic).
  • Clear channel assessment (CCA): the radio's decision that the channel is busy, which is what makes it wait.

2. PurposeWhy sharing rules exist

The licence-free bands only work if devices of many kinds tolerate each other. Wi-Fi's own rule is to listen before talking; the regulator's rules limit power, require radar detection in some 5 GHz channels, and decide who may use what, where.

3. MechanismWhat shares 2.4 GHz

The 2.4 GHz band is the most crowded. Choose a ZigBee channel and see where it sits among Wi-Fi channels 1, 6 and 11, then switch Bluetooth and a microwave oven on.

[wifi_lab model="coexist" label="Who shares the 2.4 GHz band"]

A Wi-Fi receiver declares the channel busy when it detects the start of a Wi-Fi transmission at -82 dBm or stronger (for a 20 MHz channel). It also treats any signal 20 dB stronger, at -62 dBm, as busy even if it cannot decode it. Between those two levels a non-Wi-Fi signal does not stop Wi-Fi at all: it simply adds noise, so it damages frames instead of making stations wait.

4. VisualHow much interference a receiver tolerates

The standard also says how strong an interfering signal on a neighbouring channel a receiver must survive. A faster rate tolerates less:

Modulation and coding rateAdjacent channel rejectionAlternate adjacent channel rejection
BPSK 1/216 dB32 dB
QPSK 1/213 dB29 dB
16-QAM 1/28 dB24 dB
16-QAM 3/44 dB20 dB
64-QAM 2/30 dB16 dB
64-QAM 3/4-1 dB15 dB

Receiver performance requirements for 20 MHz OFDM, from IEEE Std 802.11-2020, Table 17-18. At 64-QAM 3/4 the receiver need not tolerate an interferer even as strong as the wanted signal on the next channel; "alternate adjacent" means two channels away.

5. MathematicsOverlap and thresholds

  • Channel spacing. 2.4 GHz channels are 5 MHz apart and 20 MHz wide, so channels 5 apart do not overlap; that gives 1, 6, 11.
  • ZigBee. Channel k (11 to 26) is centred on 2405 + 5 × (k - 11) MHz. Channel 25 is at 2475 MHz, above Wi-Fi channel 11 (2462 MHz, 2452 to 2472 MHz).
  • Bluetooth. A 20 MHz Wi-Fi channel covers about 21 of the 79 channels (27%). Adaptive frequency hopping lets Bluetooth skip them.
  • Thresholds. Preamble detection at -82 dBm; energy detect at -82 + 20 = -62 dBm (20 MHz).

6. Real-world behaviourPractical rules

  • Use 1, 6 and 11 in 2.4 GHz when you have to share. A deliberately overlapping plan makes everyone's life worse than sharing a channel.
  • Move to 5 and 6 GHz where there is more space, fewer neighbours and no household devices.
  • Radar rules (DFS) in 5 GHz: a radar detected on a channel forces the network to leave it; the radar rules set a 60 second channel availability check before use, a 10 second window to move, and a 30 minute non-occupancy period.
  • Wide channels multiply the problem. A 40 MHz channel in 2.4 GHz overlaps with everything; 160 MHz in 5 GHz leaves little room.
  • Check what else is there with a spectrum analyser before blaming Wi-Fi.

7. Rules and regulationsUK first, then the EU and the US

Each domain starts with who sets the rules and then the limits. The tables open on the UK (Ofcom); switch to the EU (CEPT and ETSI) or the US (FCC). The region you choose is remembered across the lab.

[wifi_lab model="region" label="Regulatory domain switch"]

2.4 GHz

[wifi_lab model="regrules" band="2.4" label="2.4 GHz rules by region"]

[wifi_lab model="regrules" band="6" label="6 GHz rules by region"]

Practical validationProve it in a capture and on a spectrum analyser

Reading about a band is one thing; seeing it in your own evidence is the skill. These checks work with any monitor-mode capture:

  • Scan for neighbouring networks and note their channels and signal levels. Count how many share your channel and how many sit on overlapping channels.
  • Read the channel utilisation in the BSS Load element of a beacon (access points that support it announce how busy they are).
  • Run a spectrum analyser (a Wi-Fi adapter with spectrum capability, or a dedicated tool) and look for energy that does not look like Wi-Fi.
  • Question to answer: your network is on channel 6 and you see another strong network on channel 4. Would you move to channel 6 co-channel, or leave them overlapping? Why?

title: Measuring and validating
excerpt: Measurement, troubleshooting and proving a design.
content:
A network is only as good as the evidence that it works. This part is about gathering that evidence: what to measure, how to read it, and how to prove a design before people depend on it.

TopicsFrom a symptom to a sign-off

Finding the causeTroubleshootingSignal, noise, SNR, rate and retries, and what users actually feel.Design and proofEngineeringCapacity planning, surveys, standard test plans and a validation checklist.

title: Measurement, troubleshooting and quality of experience
excerpt: Signal, noise, SNR, retries and rates, and how they relate to what users feel.
content:
"The Wi-Fi is slow" is a symptom, not a diagnosis. This topic gives you the measurements that tell the likely causes apart, and a way to relate them to what the user feels.

-101 dBmthermal noise floor in 20 MHz
SNR = S - Nsignal minus noise, in dB
150 msone-way delay ITU-T G.114 regards as acceptable for most calls
retriesthe clearest sign of wasted airtime

1. DefinitionWhat to measure

  • Signal strength (RSSI or dBm): how strong the wanted signal is at the receiver. Different devices scale it differently.
  • Noise floor: the background level of unwanted energy, including thermal noise and interference.
  • Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR): signal minus noise floor, in dB. It decides which rate a link can hold.
  • Data rate and MCS: the physical rate chosen for each frame.
  • Retry rate and loss: how many frames had to be sent again.
  • Channel utilisation: how much of the time the channel is busy.
  • Throughput, latency, jitter, loss: what the application experiences. Together they make up the quality of experience (QoE).

2. PurposeWhy measure

Wi-Fi problems have many causes that feel the same to a user. A low rate can mean weak signal, high noise, a slow client or a busy channel; each needs a different fix. Measuring turns a guess into a short list.

3. MechanismFrom signal to rate

The model shows which rates a client can hold for a given signal and noise floor, using the receiver sensitivities the standard requires. Raise the noise floor and watch the usable rate fall even though the signal is unchanged.

[wifi_lab model="snr" label="Signal, noise and the rate a client can hold"]

Try this. (1) Set the signal to -60 dBm and the noise floor to -95 dBm. (2) Raise the noise floor to -80 dBm without touching the signal. (3) Notice the margin on the best rate vanishing: a strong signal on a noisy channel is not a good link.

4. VisualDoes the link meet the need?

Users do not feel signal strength; they feel video that stutters or a call that clips. Enter measured throughput, latency, jitter and loss and see which applications are served well.

[wifi_lab model="qoe" label="Quality of experience"]

5. MathematicsNoise, SNR and the budget

  • Thermal noise = -174 dBm/Hz + 10 log10(bandwidth in Hz). For 20 MHz that is -174 + 73 = -101 dBm; for 40 MHz -98 dBm; for 80 MHz -95 dBm; for 160 MHz -92 dBm. Doubling the width raises the floor by 3 dB.
  • The receiver adds its own noise (its noise figure). The standard's minimum sensitivities assume a 10 dB noise figure and 5 dB implementation margin, which is about -91 dBm in 20 MHz.
  • SNR = signal - noise floor. A signal of -60 dBm on a -95 dBm floor has 35 dB of SNR; the same signal on a -75 dBm floor has only 15 dB.
  • Retry rate = frames with the retry bit set / data frames. The airtime lost is roughly proportional.
  • Throughput can be tested with iperf3: iperf3 -c server -t 30 -P 4 for TCP with four parallel streams, -R for the reverse direction and -u -b 20M for a UDP stream at 20 Mbit/s.

6. Real-world behaviourSymptoms and likely causes

SymptomLikely causesCheck
Slow everywhereBusy channel, interference, wide channelsChannel utilisation, retry rate, noise floor
Slow in one placeWeak signal or poor SNR, a wallSignal and SNR on the spot; walk around
Drops when walkingSticky client, thin coverage between access pointsReassociation frames, signal at the moment of roam
Fine, then very slow at timesNeighbour on the same channel, a non-Wi-Fi source, DFS channel changeTime-based capture, spectrum view, DFS events
Good download, bad callsJitter or loss, not throughputPing with a long run, retry rate, QoS settings
Fast Wi-Fi, slow internetNot Wi-Fi at allTest wired to the same router; check DNS and the uplink
  • Work from the bottom up. Check the signal and noise first, then the rates and retries, then the protocol steps, then the application.
  • Change one thing at a time and measure again.
  • Measure from the client's side. The access point's view of the link is not the client's.

Practical validationProve it in a capture and on a spectrum analyser

Reading about a band is one thing; seeing it in your own evidence is the skill. These checks work with any monitor-mode capture:

  • Capture on the channel and filter for retries: wlan.fc.retry == 1. Then look at the signal in radiotap.dbm_antsignal and the data rate in wlan_radio.data_rate for the frames that are failing.
  • Find TCP problems: tcp.analysis.retransmission and tcp.analysis.lost_segment.
  • Run ping -c 100 gateway and look at the maximum and the spread of the round-trip times, not only the average.
  • Question to answer: a user has -55 dBm but only 24 Mbit/s. List three measurements you would take, in order.

  • ITU-T G.114: One-way transmission time
  • iPerf3 documentation
  • Wireshark display filter reference: IEEE 802.11 (wlan)
  • Wireshark display filter reference: radiotap

Receiver sensitivities are from IEEE Std 802.11-2020 (Tables 17-18 and 21-25) with the noise figure and margin assumptions stated in 17.3.10.2. The QoE targets are planning rules of thumb, not standards; ITU-T G.114 is the only recommendation cited. Check Wireshark field names against your version, since they are updated over time.

title: Validation and practical engineering
excerpt: Capacity and coverage planning, surveys, standard test plans and a validation checklist.
content:
Designing a Wi-Fi network means choosing where the access points go and how many, then proving that the result does what it was meant to. This topic gives you a sizing method and a validation routine.

2 limitscapacity and coverage: you need the larger
about 50%of the link rate you can really use
5 phasesplan, design, install, validate, hand over
TR-398Broadband Forum's standard test plan

1. DefinitionDesign, survey and validate

  • Predictive design: a software model of the building places access points and predicts coverage. It is only as good as its wall and material settings.
  • Site survey: measurements in the real building. A passive survey listens (signal, noise, channels); an active survey connects and tests throughput and roaming.
  • Validation: proving after installation that the network meets the agreed targets, with the evidence saved.
  • Capacity planning: making sure the access points can carry the traffic, not just reach every corner.

2. PurposeWhy this is a method, not a feeling

A network that has coverage everywhere can still be useless at 9 a.m. when a hundred people join. Capacity and coverage are two different limits, and fixing one does not fix the other. Writing the targets down first, and measuring against them at the end, is what separates engineering from guessing.

3. MechanismHow many access points?

Enter the clients, their demand, the link rate and the floor area. The capacity figure follows from the airtime lesson: only about half of a link rate is usable, and keeping access points well under full load keeps delay low.

[wifi_lab model="capacity" label="Capacity and coverage planning"]

Try this. (1) Leave the area alone and raise the number of clients until capacity becomes the limit. (2) Then increase the area and watch coverage take over. (3) Lower the share of the link rate you really get to 40% (a busy, mixed network) and see the effect.

4. VisualThe validation routine

A checklist is the simplest tool in the book. Work through the five phases and tick off each step; your progress is saved in this browser only.

[wifi_lab model="checklist" label="Wi-Fi design and validation checklist"]

5. MathematicsThe sizing rules

  • Capacity: access points = total demand / (link rate × usable share × target load). With 120 clients at 6 Mbit/s each (720 Mbit/s), a 600 Mbit/s link, 55% usable and a 50% load target: 720 / (600 × 0.55 × 0.5) = 4.4, so 5 access points.
  • Coverage: access points = floor area / the area one access point serves well. For 3000 m2 and 400 m2 each that is 7.5, so 8. You need the larger of the two numbers, here 8.
  • Channel reuse: access points that can hear each other on the same channel share its airtime, so extra access points add capacity only if they use different channels. In 2.4 GHz there are three; 5 and 6 GHz offer many more.
  • Link balance: the client's transmit power is lower than the access point's. If an access point is much louder than clients, the downlink looks fine while the uplink is poor, so match the design to the weaker side.
  • Per-client rate is roughly the usable throughput of the access point divided by the number of active clients.

6. Real-world behaviourStandard tests and RF exposure

TR-398 from the Broadband Forum defines repeatable tests of Wi-Fi equipment in a lab, so that results can be compared between products and over time. Its test cases include:

GroupTest cases
Radio performanceReceiver sensitivity
Baseline performanceMaximum connection; maximum throughput; airtime fairness
CoverageRange versus rate; spatial consistency
Multiple stationsMultiple stations performance; association and disassociation stability; downlink MU-MIMO
Stability and robustnessLong-term stability; coexistence with other access points

From TR-398 Issue 1 Corrigendum 1 (October 2019); later issues add more.

  • Acceptance criteria belong in the contract. Agree the minimum signal, SNR, throughput, roaming time and packet loss and where they apply (for example, at the edge of every working area), and test against them.
  • Test when busy. A survey at 7 a.m. in an empty building says little about a full one.
  • Document everything: final positions, channels, power levels, firmware and the survey data, so that the next person can reproduce the network.
  • RF exposure. Wi-Fi power is low, and installations must comply with the exposure guidelines the regulator applies (ICNIRP guidelines are the international reference). Keep the documentation to prove compliance when asked.

Practical validationProve it in a capture and on a spectrum analyser

Reading about a band is one thing; seeing it in your own evidence is the skill. These checks work with any monitor-mode capture:

  • Write down the targets before the survey and mark each as pass or fail afterwards.
  • Run a passive survey on all bands, an active survey with a real device and a throughput test with iperf3 -c server -t 30 -P 4 at the worst point of coverage.
  • Test roaming along every walking route with a client that is capturing, and record the reassociation time.
  • Repeat the throughput test at the busiest time of the week and compare.

Check your understandingQuick quiz

[wifi_lab model="quiz" band="eng" label="Engineering quiz"]

ReferencesSources and further reading

  • Broadband Forum: TR-398 Wi-Fi In-Premises Performance Testing
  • ICNIRP: Guidelines for limiting exposure to electromagnetic fields (100 kHz to 300 GHz), 2020
  • IEEE Std 802.11-2020 (IEEE Xplore)
  • iPerf3 documentation

The sizing method is an engineering approximation, not a standard: the usable share of the link rate and the target load are inputs you should choose from your own measurements. The TR-398 test case list was checked against the Issue 1 Corrigendum 1 document; later issues differ. RF exposure limits are set by national regulators; the ICNIRP guidelines are the international reference they commonly use.
